Official Definitions

Police/Legal numbers look comparable…

Ireland · Garda

Source: hatecrime.osce.org (police-recorded)

…but definitions disagree

shared distinctive

Ireland · Garda Germany · BKA United States · FBI Spain · Código Penal
Act criminal offence and incidents criminal offence criminal offence criminal offence
Characteristics* + age + social status, appearance — + ideology, aporophobia, illness, age
Group status actual or perceived actual or perceived actual or perceived actual or perceived

* In common: race / ethnicity, religion, disability, sexual orientation, gender (identity)

Label Typical emphasis
Hate crime Criminal act + bias motivation / protected characteristic
Hate speech Expression; legal and platform thresholds vary widely
Hate incident Broader recording (often police / civil society); not always charged

Scholars add dimensions…

It involves acts of violence and intimidation, usually directed toward already stigmatized and marginalized groups. As such, it is a mechanism of power, intended to reaffirm the precarious hierarchies that characterize a given social order. It attempts to recreate simultaneously the threatened (real or imagined) hegemony of the perpetrator’s group and the “appropriate” subordinate identity of the victim’s group.

Perry (2001: 10), in Perry (2014)

…but also disagree

…the foundations of much hate crime policy and scholarship have been built on the assumption that these are exclusively “majority versus minority” crimes. However well-intentioned, such an assumption fails to account for the acts of hate, prejudice and bigotry committed by minorities against fellow minorities, or indeed against those who might be described as majority group members.

Chakraborti (2014: 19)

…and do not reflect police categories

Germany · BKA

United States · FBI

So what?

  • You disagree
  • Police/Law disagree, on type of act and protected characteristics
  • Scholars disagree, on power, hierarchy, and who counts as a victim

What this means

→ every paper needs a definition and a generalizability-statement

→ also means we will see hardly any comparative cross-country work in this course

Part II — Underrecording & underreporting

Rising acceptance

…yet hate crime rises

Who records hate crime?

Actors involved in hate crime data collection:

  • Law enforcement agencies
  • Federal agencies
  • (Regional) government agencies
  • Human rights organizations
  • Community-based organizations & activists
  • Research institutions
  • Online platforms and technology companies

Two different problems

Underreporting

Victims (or witnesses) never tell the police / survey / platform

  • Fear of retaliation
  • Lack of trust in law enforcement
  • Perceived ineffectiveness of reporting
  • Limited awareness
  • Inadequate reporting infrastructures
  • Concerns about privacy

Underrecording

The event is known, but not flagged as hate crime

  • Inconsistent definitions
  • Inadequate recording infrastructure
  • Lack of training
  • Biases & stereotyping

So when we see rising trends…

It might mean more violence — or:

  • more willingness to report
  • better police training / mandatory fields
  • a change in definition of protected groups
  • political attention and NGO referral

Part III — Why hate crimes are different

Effects beyond the immediate victim

Why treat hate crimes different from otherwise similar non-bias offences?

  • Affect the immediate victim
  • Send message to the victim’s (perceived) community
  • Impair intergroup relations
  • Question democratic values (inclusion, equity, justice)

Outlook

Disclaimer: Two families of explanation

Individual-level

Psychological traits & offender behaviour

Cognitive and affective processes that drive perpetrators to commit hate crime

Contextual

Would-be perpetrators’ social environment

Political, cultural, sociological, and economic conditions that make bias-motivated violence more or less likely
